```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Package versions are pinned via renv (see renv.lock); run renv::restore() to install.
# Functions are called with explicit pkg:: prefixes rather than attaching via library().

# Headline numbers used in the Summary. The price shock is written by the export-price-shock
# chunk below; the land-use results by r/land_use_model/03_summarise_results.R.
shock_2035 <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"))
lum <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "land_use_country_results.csv.gz"))

# Soybean oil's share of soybean crush value (Janzen & Wang 2025; see Methods). Must match
# SOY_OIL_VALUE_SHARE in r/land_use_model/01_prepare_data.R and 00d_supply_curve.R.
soy_oil_value_share <- 4.72 / (4.72 + 8.66)

# Additional forest loss relative to BAU: BAU stock minus scenario stock, so positive = more loss.
bau <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "bau") |>
  dplyr::select(
    country, year, carbon_bau = forest_carbon_tco2, area_bau = forest_area_ha,
    palm_bau = forest_palm_oil_t, soy_bau = forest_soybeans_t
  )
loss <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_model", "vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(bau, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    carbon_loss = carbon_bau - forest_carbon_tco2, # t CO2
    area_loss = area_bau - forest_area_ha, # ha
    # t a year grown on the extra land cleared (the model's conversion; see 03_summarise_results.R)
    extra_palm_oil_t = palm_bau - forest_palm_oil_t,
    extra_soybeans_t = soy_bau - forest_soybeans_t
  )
global_loss <- loss |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(c(carbon_loss, area_loss, carbon_bau, area_bau, extra_palm_oil_t, extra_soybeans_t), sum),
    .by = c(scenario, year)
  )
gl <- function(scn, yr, var) global_loss[[var]][global_loss$scenario == scn & global_loss$year == yr]

final_year <- max(lum$year)
n_years <- final_year - min(lum$year)
country_final <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year == final_year) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = carbon_loss / sum(carbon_loss), .by = scenario) |>
  dplyr::arrange(scenario, dplyr::desc(carbon_loss))
rs_final <- country_final |> dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs")
# Countries whose additional loss peaks and then narrows by >5% (BAU later clears some of the
# same forest), among those with more than 1 Mt CO2 of additional loss.
gap_peaks <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    peak = max(carbon_loss),
    peak_year = year[which.max(carbon_loss)],
    final = carbon_loss[year == final_year],
    .by = country
  )
n_narrowing <- sum(gap_peaks$peak > 1e6 & gap_peaks$final < 0.95 * gap_peaks$peak)
mys <- gap_peaks[gap_peaks$country == "Malaysia", ]

# ILUC carbon intensity: additional forest carbon loss after T years of fuel use, divided by T
# years of VO-RD energy at the 2035 level. Annual VO-RD energy is ICCT's 2035 VO-RD share of
# shipping energy (Table 1), saved by the scrape-icct-table-1 chunk below.
icct_saved <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"))
icct_2035 <- icct_saved[icct_saved$year == 2035, ]
vord_mj_2035 <- icct_2035$vord_pct_energy_demand / 100 * icct_2035$shipping_energy_demand_ej * 1e12
vord_direct_ci <- 42.3 # g CO2e/MJ, soy VO-RD (Seber & Pavlenko 2025, p. 6)
fossil_baseline_ci <- 93.3 # g CO2e/MJ, 2008 baseline (Seber & Pavlenko 2025, p. 1)
accounting_years <- c(20, 25, 30)
headline_years <- 25
iluc <- expand.grid(
  scenario = c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_model"),
  years = accounting_years,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
iluc$carbon_loss <- mapply(
  function(scn, yrs) gl(scn, min(lum$year) + yrs, "carbon_loss"),
  iluc$scenario, iluc$years
)
iluc$g_per_mj <- iluc$carbon_loss * 1e6 / (iluc$years * vord_mj_2035)
iluc <- iluc[order(iluc$scenario, iluc$years), ]
il <- function(scn, yrs) iluc$g_per_mj[iluc$scenario == scn & iluc$years == yrs]
# Where an ILUC value sits relative to ICCT's 62 and Chen et al.'s 84.1 g CO2e/MJ, for the text.
vs_benchmarks <- function(x) if (x < 62) "below both" else if (x > 84.1) "above both" else "between them"

# Closest benchmark: Chen et al.'s ILUC from forest biomass carbon alone, the only pool we count. They
# study forest-to-palm conversion in Indonesia and Malaysia only, so we also give those countries' part
# of our headline value.
chen_biomass_iluc <- 58.7 # g CO2e/MJ, biomass carbon (AGB + BGB) (Chen et al. 2026, Table 1, p. 13)
iluc_of <- function(countries, scn = "vo_rs", yrs = headline_years) {
  rows <- loss$scenario == scn & loss$year == min(lum$year) + yrs & loss$country %in% countries
  sum(loss$carbon_loss[rows]) * 1e6 / (yrs * vord_mj_2035)
}
im_iluc <- iluc_of(c("Indonesia", "Malaysia"))
drc_iluc <- iluc_of("Democratic Republic of the Congo")

# The emLab model's own demand elasticities (K_elas_pivot_full.Rdata, saved by r/audit_crop_mix.R). Its
# price calculation (00c_run_cobweb.R) pairs them with its supply from newly cleared forest. The price
# shock below pairs the model's supply with its demand elasticity for palm; it is not run through the model.
model_demand <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "model_demand_elasticities.csv"))
eps_d_model <- stats::setNames(model_demand$elasticity, model_demand$crop)
pct_delta_p_model_own <- shock_2035$demand_share_pct / (shock_2035$eps_s_model - eps_d_model[["Oil, palm"]])

# Crop attribution: palm-only and soy-only runs of the Roberts & Schlenker shock. They sum to the joint run
# to within the interaction term reported here.
crop_split <- c(
  palm = gl("vo_rs_palm", final_year, "carbon_loss"),
  soy = gl("vo_rs_soy", final_year, "carbon_loss")
)
interaction_pct <- 100 * (gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") - sum(crop_split)) /
  gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss")

fmt1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
fmt0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")
# Elasticities: two decimals from 0.05 up, two significant digits below, with a true minus sign.
fmt_el <- function(x) {
  sub("^-", "−", ifelse(abs(x) >= 0.05, formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2), formatC(x, digits = 2, format = "fg")))
}
# Country names as they read mid-sentence ("the Democratic Republic of the Congo").
the_country <- function(x) {
  ifelse(grepl("^(Democratic Republic|Republic of|Central African Republic|United States|United Kingdom|United Republic|Philippines|Netherlands|Gambia|Ivory Coast|Solomon Islands)", x), paste("the", x), x)
}

# Figures: one ggplot2 theme and one set of colors throughout. Scenarios and crops keep the same
# colors in every figure; magnitude on maps uses viridisLite's magma, reversed so darker means
# more loss (the ends are trimmed so the lightest step stays visible on the gray land).
col_surface <- "#fcfcfb"
col_land <- "#ecebe6"
col_scenario <- c(rs = "#2a78d6", model = "#eb6834")
scenario_labels <- c(rs = "Roberts & Schlenker", model = "Roberts & Schlenker demand, emLab model supply")
col_crop <- c("Oil palm" = "#1baf7a", "Soybeans" = "#eda100")
map_ramp <- function(n) viridisLite::magma(n, direction = -1, begin = 0.1, end = 0.95)

theme_report <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = col_surface, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
theme_map <- function() {
  theme_report() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.justification = "center"
    )
}

# Country outlines (Natural Earth 1:110m), as vertices; see r/make_basemap.R.
basemap <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "natural_earth", "ne_110m_admin_0_countries.csv.gz"))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Preliminary and exploratory

This is a prototype, and its numbers are rough. Read them as the likely scale of the effect rather than as estimates for policy, regulation or carbon accounting, and expect them to change as the work develops.

Three things matter most. The price shock that drives everything else comes from a simple formula meant for small changes, while marine demand would equal `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of today's world vegetable-oil production. The land-use model that turns prices into forest loss has a much weaker supply response than published estimates, so the two halves of the analysis don't fully line up ([Methods](#sec-model-supply), [check](#sec-results-check)). And the country results are the least reliable part: we apply one world price everywhere, and the model's broad crop zones send some of the palm response to Central Africa ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)). We also count only carbon in forest biomass, so peat and soil carbon are missing. The [Caveats](#sec-caveats) section has the full list.
:::

## Summary

ICCT estimates that meeting the Net-Zero Framework's Base target at least cost takes about `r fmt0(shock_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters)` billion liters of virgin vegetable oil a year for marine renewable diesel (VO-RD) by 2035 [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. That is `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflower oil.

Supply and demand elasticities measure how much production and consumption change when prices rise by 1%. With Roberts & Schlenker's widely used estimates for staple crops [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279], our primary scenario, that demand raises vegetable-oil prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. A second scenario, the emLab-model scenario, keeps their demand elasticity but uses the supply elasticity implied by emLab's land-use model (`r formatC(shock_2035$eps_s_model, digits = 2, format = "fg")`; see [Methods](#sec-model-supply)), the model we use to turn prices into forest loss. Prices then rise `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`%, because the model adds almost no new supply and other buyers must give up nearly all of the oil the ships use. That pairing overstates the shock: the model's own price calculation pairs its supply with much more responsive demand, which would give `r fmt0(pct_delta_p_model_own)`% ([Appendix C](#sec-model-demand)). Both shocks come from a linear approximation stretched far beyond its range, so we use them to size the model's inputs, not as price forecasts.

The emLab model prices palm as oil but soybeans as whole beans, and oil is about 35% of a crushed soybean's value [@janzen2025, Fig. 2]. Holding meal prices fixed, the primary scenario raises palm oil prices `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%.

At those prices, the emLab model clears an extra `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 15 years compared with business as usual (BAU), releasing `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. Over its full `r n_years`-year run the totals are `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha and `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. The palm price increase causes `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the extra loss. The emLab-model scenario loses `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs_model", final_year, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss"))` times as much carbon. In the primary scenario, `r the_country(rs_final$country[1])` and `r the_country(rs_final$country[2])` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:2]))`% of the loss, but the country split is the least reliable part of the analysis.

Spread over `r headline_years` years of fuel use, the extra loss comes to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g CO₂ per MJ of VO-RD in the primary scenario (`r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 20))` over 20 years, `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 30))` over 30) and `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_model", 25))` in the emLab-model scenario. Adding VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ [@seber2025, p. 6] gives `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))` and `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_model", 25))` g/MJ, against a fossil baseline of `r fossil_baseline_ci`.

For comparison, ICCT has used an ILUC value of 62 g CO₂e/MJ [@sturrup2026, p. 10], and @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] estimate 84.1 for palm. Our primary value is `r vs_benchmarks(il("vo_rs", 25))`, and the emLab-model value is `r vs_benchmarks(il("vo_rs_model", 25))`. Both benchmarks are ILUC alone, like ours, so ICCT's 62 compares with our `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))`, not with our total of `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))`. We count only forest biomass carbon, so the closest benchmark is Chen et al.'s biomass carbon alone, `r chen_biomass_iluc` g CO₂e/MJ; peat added another 47.5 [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13]. Our primary value is close to it, but only `r fmt1(im_iluc)` g/MJ of ours comes from Indonesia and Malaysia, the two countries they study, and `r fmt1(drc_iluc)` from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The agreement is partly a coincidence.

## Background

### The IMO Net-Zero Framework

In April 2025 the International Maritime Organization approved draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI [@sturrup2026, p. 1] that set greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity (GFI) targets for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above. GFI is well-to-wake g CO₂e/MJ, measured against a 2008 baseline of 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]. The Base target tightens from a 4% cut in 2028 to 30% by 2035, and the stricter Direct Compliance target from 17% to 43%. Ships above the Base target pay \$380 per tonne of excess CO₂e (Tier 2), and ships between the two targets pay \$100 (Tier 1) [@seber2025, pp. 1–2].

As of October 2026 the framework has not been adopted. At an extraordinary session in October 2025, a Saudi Arabian motion to adjourn for a year passed with 57 votes, including 15 countries that had backed the framework in April [@carbonbrief2026]. MEPC 84 (27 April–1 May 2026) kept the April 2025 text as the basis for further work, invited alternatives, and scheduled two more meetings of its intersessional working group on greenhouse gases [@carbonbrief2026; @abs2026mepc84, p. 4]. The first, ISWG-GHG 22 (1–4 September 2026), ended without agreement [@shipandbunker2026]. The sharpest split is over the GHG price and the central IMO fund it pays into. By one observer's count of the countries that spoke, 38 supported them and 17, mostly oil producers, opposed them, and the United States again rejected any IMO-run fund [@shipandbunker2026]. The early GFI trajectory and the rules for pooling compliance surpluses are also unresolved [@maritimeexecutive2026]. Japan's proposal to replace the fund with direct payments from shipowners won little support in September [@maritimeexecutive2026]; its revised version drops the fund and has ships cover shortfalls by buying surplus units from other ships [@marineinsight2026].

The working group meets again 23–27 November, followed by MEPC 85 (30 November–3 December). If MEPC 85 agrees, the extraordinary session resumes on 4 December 2026 and could vote that day [@abs2026mepc84, p. 4; @shipandbunker2026]. Whatever is adopted may differ from the April 2025 text we start from: a gentler early trajectory would mean less biofuel demand, and dropping the GHG price would change the compliance costs that set the fuel mix.

The framework judges fuels on their direct life-cycle emissions only. The IMO's life-cycle guidelines treat ILUC as too uncertain to give each fuel a number, and handle it through a qualitative, risk-based approach instead [@imo2024lca, paras. 4.12–4.13]. MEPC 84 supported this in principle and asked for more quantitative analysis by MEPC 85 [@abs2026mepc84, p. 6]. Because blending biofuel costs less than the \$380 Tier 2 penalty, the cheapest strategy is to blend just enough to meet the Base target. In ICCT's least-cost mix, used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) runs out at about 5% of shipping energy and virgin vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) covers the rest, reaching 46% of shipping energy by 2035 [@seber2025, p. 4 and Table 1, p. 5].

ICCT's Table 1 gives the mix for each year from 2028 to 2035. We read it straight from the PDF; its last column, virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, is our demand shift.

```{r}
#| label: scrape-icct-table-1

pdf_path <- file.path(
  "data",
  "icct_biofuel_demand_report",
  "ID-450-Vegetable-Oil_research-brief_final.pdf"
)

# Extract page 5 as text and keep only the data rows (years 2028–2035)
page5 <- pdftools::pdf_text(pdf_path)[5]
lines <- stringr::str_trim(stringr::str_split(page5, "\n")[[1]])
data_lines <- stringr::str_subset(lines, "^20(2[89]|3[0-5])\\b")

# Each data row yields exactly 10 numeric tokens:
#   year, shipping demand, base target, fossil LNG %,
#   UCO-RD %, UCO-RD bl, VO-RD %, VO-RD bl, UCO demand bl, VO demand bl
nums <- stringr::str_extract_all(data_lines, "[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*")
mat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nums, function(x) as.numeric(x[seq_len(10)])))

icct_table_1 <- tibble::as_tibble(mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
names(icct_table_1) <- c(
  "year",
  "shipping_energy_demand_ej",
  "base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj",
  "fossil_lng_pct",
  "ucord_pct_energy_demand",
  "ucord_billion_liters",
  "vord_pct_energy_demand",
  "vord_billion_liters",
  "uco_demand_billion_liters",
  "vo_demand_billion_liters"
)

icct_table_1 <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

# Saved for the setup chunk, which needs the 2035 VO-RD energy for the ILUC calculation.
utils::write.csv(icct_table_1, file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(
  icct_table_1 |>
    dplyr::select(
      year,
      shipping_energy_demand_ej,
      base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj,
      ucord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_billion_liters,
      vo_demand_billion_liters
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "Shipping energy (EJ)",
    "Base target (g CO₂e/MJ)",
    "UCO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD fuel (billion L)",
    "Virgin VO feedstock (billion L)"
  ),
  caption = "ICCT Table 1, selected columns [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, the last column, is the demand shock D."
)
```

The direct carbon intensities behind the mix:

| Fuel | Life-cycle carbon intensity (g CO₂e/MJ) |
|---|---|
| 2008 baseline | 93.3 |
| Heavy fuel oil (HFO) | 92.8 |
| Fossil LNG | 85.7 |
| Soy vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) | 42.3 |
| Soy FAME biodiesel | 35.7 |
| Used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) | 13.1 |

: Direct life-cycle carbon intensities used by ICCT: 2008 baseline (p. 1); fossil LNG, 85.65 (p. 2); HFO, 92.78, soy VO-RD, soy FAME (35.74) and UCO-RD (p. 6) [@seber2025]. None include indirect land-use change.

### Indirect land-use change

Indirect land-use change (ILUC) happens when biofuel demand raises crop prices and the higher prices lead to forest being cleared for farmland elsewhere. Those emissions fall outside the fuel's own supply chain, so a fuel mix can meet the GFI targets on paper while adding emissions nobody counts. Our steps:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["IMO Net-Zero Framework"] --> F["Marine VO-RD demand<br/><i>ICCT cost-optimization</i>"]
  F --> B["Virgin vegetable-oil demand<br/><i>1.22 kg oil per kg RD</i>"]
  B --> C["Vegetable-oil price shock<br/><i>this report</i>"]
  C --> D["Forest loss by country<br/><i>emLab land-use model</i>"]
  D --> E["ILUC carbon intensity<br/><i>this report</i>"]
```

ICCT converts renewable diesel to oil at 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel [@seber2025, p. 3, note 9].

Published ILUC estimates for vegetable-oil biofuels vary widely:

| Source | Approach | ILUC result |
|---|---|---|
| ICCT climate & revenue brief [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11] | Fixed factor applied to ICCT's demand projection | 62 g CO₂e/MJ; ~285 Mt CO₂e/yr by 2035; ~950 Mt CO₂e over 2028–2035 |
| U.S. EPA model comparison [@epa2023mce, Table 7.7-1, p. 113] | Five models, soybean-oil biodiesel shock | Land-use change: 10 to 295 kg CO₂e/MMBTU (GCAM: 62) |
| @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] | Econometric estimates of demand → price → deforestation for palm, 2002–2018 | 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ (90% CI 48.7–113.5) |
| GLOBIOM for the EU [@valin2015, p. x] | Global economic land-use model, emissions spread over 20 years | 231 g CO₂e/MJ for palm oil, 150 for soybean oil |

: ICCT takes its 62 from the EPA model comparison [@sturrup2026, p. 10]. The only 62 in the EPA's results table is GCAM's land-use-change value, in kg CO₂e/MMBTU (≈ 59 g CO₂e/MJ), so we assume that is the source. Every value here is ILUC alone, without the fuel's direct emissions. ICCT adds its 62, weighted by VO-RD's share of shipping energy (62 × 46% ≈ 28.5 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035), to the fleet's Base-target GFI [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11], which puts the ILUC-adjusted fleet GFI at 93.86 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035, above the fossil baseline [@sturrup2026, Table A1, p. 15].

Like Chen et al., we estimate how much the demand shift raises prices and then use an econometric land-use model to turn prices into forest loss, rather than assume an ILUC factor.

## Methods and assumptions

The analysis has four steps:

1. Turn ICCT's 2035 vegetable-oil demand into a price shock, in two scenarios: Roberts & Schlenker's supply and demand elasticities (primary), and their demand elasticity with the emLab model's own supply elasticity (the emLab-model scenario).
2. Translate the shock into prices for the emLab model's crops.
3. Run the model with baseline and shocked prices, both at a zero carbon price, and take the difference in forest loss.
4. Spread the extra emissions over the fuel used, to get g CO₂ per MJ.

### From demand to a price shock {#sec-price-shock}

When demand shifts out, the price rises by roughly the size of the shift divided by the gap between the supply and demand elasticities [@roberts2013, Table 1, panel C, p. 2279]:

$$ \%\Delta P \;\approx\; \underbrace{\frac{D}{Q_0}}_{\text{demand shift}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_s - \varepsilon_d}}_{\text{multiplier } M} $$

where $D$ is marine virgin vegetable-oil demand and $Q_0$ is baseline world production. The supply elasticity $\varepsilon_s > 0$ is the percentage rise in production when prices rise 1%, and the demand elasticity $\varepsilon_d < 0$ is the percentage change in consumption. The multiplier $M$ is the percentage price rise for each percentage point of demand shift: the less supply and demand respond, the larger it is.

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Marine virgin vegetable-oil demand, 2035 ($D$) | 139.3 billion L | ICCT [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5] |
| Baseline market ($Q_0$) | ≈ 204 Mt: world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflowerseed oil, 2024/25 | USDA Production, Supply and Distribution (PSD) database [@usdapsd] |
| Oil density, to put $D$ and $Q_0$ in the same units | 0.92 kg/L | ICCT's own soy-oil conversion: 12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L (0.919 kg/L) [@seber2025, Table A1, p. 7] |
| Demand elasticity ($\varepsilon_d$) | −0.05 | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279] (range −0.03 to −0.07) |
| Supply elasticity, primary ($\varepsilon_s$) | 0.10 | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279] (range 0.09–0.12) |
| Supply elasticity, emLab-model scenario ($\varepsilon_s$) | `r formatC(shock_2035$eps_s_model, digits = 2, format = "fg")`: the emLab model's own one-year supply elasticity for vegetable oil | Our estimate ([below](#sec-model-supply)) |
| Elasticities of Chen et al., for comparison only | $\varepsilon_s \approx 0.12$ (long-run 0.10 for palm and 0.13 for competing oil crops, weighted by production), $\varepsilon_d = -0.284$ (the inverse of their estimated demand flexibility, the price change per 1% change in quantity, of −3.523) | @chen2026 [Fig. 2B, rows 3–4, p. 4; Table S1, col. 3] |
| Demand year | 2035 only | Our choice: the final year of the ICCT projection |
| "Beyond marginal" flag | demand share > 25% | Our own cutoff for where the approximation gets unreliable (not from a source) |

: Inputs to the price shock. The primary multiplier is $M \approx 6.7$; with the emLab model's supply elasticity, $M \approx 20$. Chen et al.'s elasticities would give $M \approx 2.5$.

$Q_0$ is world production of the four oils in 2024/25, summed across countries from USDA's PSD oilseeds data, downloaded on 31 July 2026 [@usdapsd]. USDA revises PSD continuously, so a later download may differ slightly.

```{r}
#| label: psd-q0

psd_zip_path <- file.path("data", "usda_psd_oilseeds", "psd_oilseeds_csv.zip")
psd <- utils::read.csv(unz(psd_zip_path, "psd_oilseeds.csv"))

q0_market_year <- 2024 # marketing year 2024/25

psd_four_oils <- psd |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Commodity_Description %in%
      c("Oil, Palm", "Oil, Soybean", "Oil, Rapeseed", "Oil, Sunflowerseed"),
    Attribute_Description == "Production",
    Market_Year == q0_market_year
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    production_mt = sum(Value) / 1000, # reported in 1000 MT
    .by = Commodity_Description
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(production_mt))
q0_mt <- sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt) # ~204 Mt

knitr::kable(
  psd_four_oils,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Commodity", "World production, 2024/25 (million t)"),
  caption = paste0(
    "World production of the four major vegetable oils (USDA PSD). Total: ",
    round(sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt), 1),
    " million t."
  )
)
```

Notes on these choices:

- Vegetable oils substitute for one another, so we treat them as one market even though ships would burn soy oil [@chen2026, p. 4]. Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities describe the world market for calories from maize, wheat, rice and soybeans; we use them as a stand-in for vegetable oils.
- We keep the supply elasticity in the multiplier because the emLab model takes prices as given, so the price we give it should already reflect the supply response. Dropping it from the primary scenario would give $M = 20$ and triple the shock, which is roughly what the emLab-model scenario does.
- The formula is a linear approximation, and marine demand is a large share of the market from about 2032, so the 2035 shock gives the scale of the effect, not its size. Roberts & Schlenker also note that, allowing for uncertainty in the elasticities, the expected multiplier is higher than the one from their central estimates [@roberts2013, p. 2280].
- Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity is the output response to the price expected at planting, a year ahead. They argue it is not just a short-run lower bound, because farmers expect price changes to persist [@roberts2013, p. 2285]. Oil palm, by contrast, takes about four years to start fruiting [@chen2026, p. 4].
- Crushing soybeans also yields meal, whose revenue relieves some of the pressure on oil prices. Roberts & Schlenker cut their price effect by a third when a third of the calories return as animal feed [@roberts2013, p. 2280]. We make no such adjustment, so on this count our shock is too high.
- With each paper's own elasticities, the formula reproduces its headline price effect ([Results](#sec-results-price)).

### The emLab model's own supply elasticity {#sec-model-supply}

The emLab model has a supply response of its own: a higher price raises the potential farm revenue of each grid cell (about 9 km across), more forest is cleared, and some of the cleared land grows the crop. We measure it by raising prices, simulating forward from 2020 at a zero carbon price, and counting the extra crop grown on the extra forest cleared, the way the emLab model's own code does: cleared area × the share of the cell's 2000–2020 forest loss that became cropland × the cell's crop mix × yield.

The price shock needs a single supply elasticity for the whole vegetable-oil market, but the model has two oil crops, priced in different units. We combine them the same way the price shock enters the model:

1. A 1% rise in the vegetable-oil price raises the palm price 1% and the soybean price `r formatC(soy_oil_value_share, format = "f", digits = 2)`%, because soybeans are priced as whole beans and oil is about a third of their value (see the [mapping](#sec-mapping)).
2. We simulate one year and count the extra palm oil and the extra soybeans grown on newly cleared land.
3. We put both in tonnes of oil. Palm is already counted as oil; soybeans convert at 11 lb of oil per 60 lb bushel, or `r fmt0(100 * 11 / 60)`% [@janzen2025, Fig. 2]. Adding the two gives the extra vegetable oil.
4. We divide that extra oil by world production of all four oils in 2024/25 [@usdapsd], $Q_0$ = `r fmt0(q0_mt)` Mt, and then by the 1% price change. Rapeseed and sunflower aren't in the model, so they add no supply, but they stay in $Q_0$ because the price formula uses the four-oil market.

We average a 1% rise and a 1% fall, which gives the elasticity at today's prices. We also trace the whole curve, from −50% to +1,500%, and repeat the calculation 5, 10 and 25 years out. For comparison with Chen et al.'s crop-specific estimates, we also raise each crop's price on its own, and measure palm oil against world palm oil production and soybeans against world soybean production.

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-curve
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

# Extra palm oil and soybean production on the extra forest cleared after a permanent price
# change, relative to BAU (r/land_use_model/00d_supply_curve.R), in each experiment's own
# commodity: palm oil, soybeans, or vegetable oil (palm oil plus the oil in the soybeans).
model_supply <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "land_use_supply_curve.csv"))
vo_rows <- model_supply$experiment == "vegetable_oil"
stopifnot(
  "00d_supply_curve.R must map the soybean shock with soy_oil_value_share" = isTRUE(all.equal(
    model_supply$pct_change_soy[vo_rows], soy_oil_value_share * model_supply$pct_change_palm[vo_rows]
  ))
)

soy_oil_per_bean <- 11 / 60 # lb of oil per 60 lb bushel (Janzen & Wang 2025)
psd_world_mt <- function(commodity) {
  sum(psd$Value[psd$Commodity_Description == commodity & psd$Attribute_Description == "Production" &
    psd$Market_Year == q0_market_year]) / 1000
}
world_mt <- c(palm = psd_world_mt("Oil, Palm"), soy = psd_world_mt("Oilseed, Soybean"), vegetable_oil = q0_mt)
to_mt <- function(experiment, palm_t, soy_t) {
  ifelse(experiment == "palm", palm_t,
    ifelse(experiment == "soy", soy_t, palm_t + soy_oil_per_bean * soy_t)
  ) / 1e6
}
model_supply <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    extra_mt = to_mt(experiment, extra_palm_oil_t, extra_soybeans_t),
    extra_mt_upper = to_mt(experiment, extra_palm_oil_t_upper, extra_soybeans_t_upper),
    pct_supply = 100 * extra_mt / world_mt[experiment],
    pct_supply_upper = 100 * extra_mt_upper / world_mt[experiment]
  )
supply_at <- function(exp, pct, yrs = 1) {
  model_supply[model_supply$experiment == exp & model_supply$pct_change == pct & model_supply$years == yrs, ]
}

# Point elasticities at baseline prices, from the -1% and +1% runs.
model_elasticity <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::filter(abs(pct_change) == 1) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    eps = (pct_supply[pct_change == 1] - pct_supply[pct_change == -1]) / 2,
    eps_upper = (pct_supply_upper[pct_change == 1] - pct_supply_upper[pct_change == -1]) / 2,
    .by = c(experiment, years)
  )
eps_model <- function(exp, yrs = 1, col = "eps") {
  model_elasticity[[col]][model_elasticity$experiment == exp & model_elasticity$years == yrs]
}

crop_labels <- c(palm = "Palm oil (palm price)", soy = "Soybeans (soybean price)", vegetable_oil = "Vegetable oil (both prices)")
col_horizon <- c("1 year" = "#2a78d6", "25 years" = "#8f8d86")
curve_plot <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::filter(years %in% c(1, 25)) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(expand.grid(experiment = names(crop_labels), years = c(1, 25), pct_change = 0, extra_mt = 0)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    horizon = ifelse(years == 1, "1 year", "25 years"),
    panel = factor(crop_labels[experiment], levels = crop_labels)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(experiment, years, pct_change)

ggplot2::ggplot(curve_plot, ggplot2::aes(extra_mt, pct_change, colour = horizon, linetype = horizon)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c3c2b9", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#c3c2b9", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_horizon, name = "After the price change:") +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c("1 year" = "solid", "25 years" = "22"), name = "After the price change:") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "The emLab model's supply curves",
    x = "Extra production relative to BAU (Mt a year)",
    y = "Change in price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-elasticity

fmt_eps <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 2, format = "fg")
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Supply of" = c("Palm oil", "Soybeans", "Vegetable oil"),
    "Price changed" = c("Palm", "Soybeans", paste0("Both: palm +1%, soybeans +", formatC(soy_oil_value_share, format = "f", digits = 2), "% (per 1% vegetable-oil price)")),
    "1 year" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 1)),
    "5 years" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 5)),

    "25 years" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 25)),

  ),
  row.names = FALSE,

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-numbers
#| include: false

# Numbers for the text: first-year clearing under BAU and from a +1% vegetable-oil price change,
# and the share of that extra clearing the model counts as cropland.
bau_year1_ha <- sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) - sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2021])
veg_1pct <- supply_at("vegetable_oil", 1)
cropland_share <- veg_1pct$extra_mt / veg_1pct$extra_mt_upper
veg_max <- supply_at("vegetable_oil", max(model_supply$pct_change))
```

The model's one-year supply elasticity for vegetable oil is `r fmt_eps(eps_model("vegetable_oil"))`. To see where that comes from: a 1% rise in the vegetable-oil price adds `r fmt0(veg_1pct$extra_palm_oil_t)` t of palm oil and `r fmt0(veg_1pct$extra_soybeans_t)` t of soybeans (`r fmt0(soy_oil_per_bean * veg_1pct$extra_soybeans_t)` t of oil) in the first year. That is `r fmt0(veg_1pct$extra_palm_oil_t + soy_oil_per_bean * veg_1pct$extra_soybeans_t)` t of vegetable oil, or `r formatC(100 * (veg_1pct$extra_palm_oil_t + soy_oil_per_bean * veg_1pct$extra_soybeans_t) / (q0_mt * 1e6), digits = 2, format = "fg")`% of the `r fmt0(q0_mt)` Mt world market, about `r fmt0(signif(0.10 / eps_model("vegetable_oil"), 1))` times less than Roberts & Schlenker's 0.10 would give. Four things keep it small:

- A 1% rise in vegetable-oil prices clears only `r fmt0(veg_1pct$extra_forest_loss_ha)` ha more forest in the first year, against `r fmt1(bau_year1_ha / 1e6)` Mha cleared under BAU.
- The model counts about `r fmt0(100 * cropland_share)`% of that extra clearing as cropland, and only the palm and soybean share of each cell's crop mix as palm and soybeans. Even counting every extra hectare as cropland would only raise the elasticity to `r fmt_eps(eps_model("vegetable_oil", col = "eps_upper"))`.
- New cropland on cleared forest is the model's only source of supply. Higher yields, expansion onto land that isn't forest, crop switching and the other oil crops are all outside it, while published elasticities include them.
- Each cell gets the crop mix of its whole agro-ecological zone (from FAO's Global Agro-Ecological Zones, GAEZ), which suits a model built to price carbon against a cell's total revenue. For a shock to palm and soybeans alone, though, it caps palm at 17.5% of any cell's crop mix, even in Riau, a palm frontier in central Sumatra. In Indonesia and Malaysia, the palm supply from forest that this gives is about 100 times smaller than Chen et al.'s econometric estimate implies. This is probably the biggest factor, and it suggests that reading a crop supply elasticity off the model is not a use it was built for ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)).

Supply builds over time as the higher price keeps clearing faster: after 25 years the elasticity is `r fmt_eps(eps_model("vegetable_oil", 25))`. The one-year curve flattens a little at high prices; over a +`r fmt0(veg_max$pct_change)`% change the average elasticity is `r fmt_eps(veg_max$pct_supply / veg_max$pct_change)`.

The emLab-model scenario uses the one-year vegetable-oil elasticity at baseline prices, the counterpart of Roberts & Schlenker's one-year response.


### Mapping the shock to the model's crops {#sec-mapping}

Following @chen2026 [p. 3], we apply the same percentage shock to all vegetable-oil prices. Palm oil prices respond to production shocks in competing oil crops about as strongly as to shocks in palm itself (their Fig. 2A, p. 4), and the four oil prices move together in the long run, almost one-for-one [cointegrating coefficients of 1.04 for soybean, 1.01 for canola and 0.86 for sunflower oil, @chen2026, Table S5]. Other work adds nuance: @cui2017 [abstract] find that soy oil diverted to US biodiesel is replaced mostly by palm oil, and @santeramo2017 [p. 13] finds a mix of substitutes and complements that varies by oil and region. Letting each oil's price respond differently would be a sensible refinement.

Only two of the model's 17 crops produce vegetable oil: palm, priced per tonne of palm oil, and soybeans, priced per tonne of beans. According to the emLab model's code, their baseline prices are observed 2020 prices: \$768/t for palm and \$415/t for soybeans, both within 2% of the World Bank's 2020 averages (\$752/t and \$407/t). Soybean oil averaged \$838/t that year [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1].

| Model crop | Shock | Why | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palm oil | $\%\Delta P$ | The model prices palm as oil | — |
| Soybeans | $s \times \%\Delta P$, with $s = 0.353$ | Oil is only part of a soybean's value, and we hold the meal price fixed. $s = \$4.72 / (\$4.72 + \$8.66)$, from the 2007–2025 average per-bushel values of soybean oil and meal | @janzen2025 [Fig. 2] (USDA AMS Illinois plant prices; 11 lb oil and 48 lb meal per bushel) |
| Rapeseed/canola, sunflower | not modeled | Not among the model's crops | — |

: How the oil-price shock enters the emLab model.

Two checks on $s$: Irwin's 2007–2017 averages (\$4.43 oil, \$8.33 meal) give 0.347 [@irwin2017, Fig. 3], and World Bank 2020 prices (\$838/t oil, \$394/t meal) give 0.33 [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1]. The share swings week to week: between 25% and 35% over 2013–2020, rarely below 35% since, and briefly 50% in 2021 and 2025 [@janzen2025, Fig. 3]. It is an accounting share, not an estimate of how soybean prices respond.

Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model, so their land-use response is missing and ILUC is understated. We still define $Q_0$ over all four oils, because they compete in one market; using palm and soy alone would inflate the demand share. In 2024/25, 86% of world rapeseed came from Canada, the EU, China, India, Australia and Russia, and 90% of sunflowerseed from Russia, Ukraine, the EU, Argentina, Kazakhstan and China [@usdapsd], so most of the missing response is probably outside tropical forests. We have not quantified it.

### The emLab land-use model {#sec-land-use-model}

We use emLab's global deforestation model; [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes) lists every change we made to its code.

It is a statistical model of the share of each grid cell's forest cleared each year, as a function of the cell's potential farm revenue and its remaining tree cover, estimated on 2001–2020 data (29.1 million cell-years). It controls for each cell's fixed characteristics and for conditions in each country and year (technically, a fractional logit with cell and country-by-year fixed effects). A cell's revenue is crop price minus transport cost, times attainable yield, averaged over the 17 crops by their share of harvested area and converted to a present value at a 5% discount rate. Transport cost scales with travel time to port and the crude-oil price.

From 2020 tree cover, the model steps forward a year at a time to 2171 over 1,450,769 grid cells (1/12°, about 9 km across) in 154 countries. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, and cleared forest never grows back.

All runs use a zero carbon price, and BAU uses 2020 prices. The primary run raises palm oil prices by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices by `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%; the emLab-model run, by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`% and `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`%. Two more runs apply the primary shock to palm and to soybeans separately, to split the loss by crop. Prices jump once, in the first model year, and stay there, so model year 2035 means 15 years after the shock, not the calendar year.

Forest carbon (t CO₂) is tree cover times carbon density, and forest area (ha) is carbon divided by density, using the model's own conversion. We count lost forest carbon as emissions, which leaves out peat, soil carbon and lost future sequestration. As a sanity check, the model has `r fmt0(sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 2020, `r fmt0(100 * sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 4.06e9)`% of FAO's 4.06 billion ha [@fao2020fra, p. 1]; the two define forest differently.

We use the model's input data unmodified, and summarize its results by country and by 0.5° grid square; [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes) gives the file details. Map outlines are Natural Earth's 1:110m countries [@naturalearth].

### ILUC carbon intensity {#sec-iluc-method}

We spread the extra emissions over an accounting period of $T$ years of fuel use:

$$ \text{ILUC}_T = \frac{\Delta C(T)}{T \times E} $$

where $\Delta C(T)$ is the cumulative extra forest carbon loss $T$ years after the shock, and $E$ is one year of VO-RD energy at the 2035 level: ICCT's 46.0% VO-RD share of 10.0 EJ of shipping energy, or 4.60 EJ [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Working forward from the feedstock instead (139.3 billion L of oil at 0.92 kg/L, 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel and 43,980 MJ per tonne of fuel) gives 4.62 EJ [@seber2025, pp. 3 and 6, Table A1]. Because the model applies the 2035 demand level from its first year, $T$ years means $T$ years of fuel use at that level, not a span of calendar years.

There is no standard $T$. The EU uses 20 years [@valin2015, p. 3] and the US EPA 30 [@chen2026, p. 13]. We report 20, 25 and 30 and headline 25, the period Chen et al. use to match the oil palm replanting cycle [@chen2026, p. 13], so our number compares directly with their 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ. ICCT's 62 g CO₂e/MJ comes from the EPA's model comparison, which divides cumulative 2020–2050 emissions by cumulative fuel use over the same years [@epa2023mce, pp. 83–84], so it is closest to our 30-year value.

The result counts only CO₂ from forest biomass. We split it by country using each country's share of the extra loss, and by crop using the palm-only and soy-only runs.

## Results

### Vegetable-oil price shock {#sec-results-price}

```{r}
#| label: price-shock-parameters

# Q0 (psd-q0 chunk) in billion liters at 0.92 kg/L, ICCT's own soy-oil conversion
# (12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L, ICCT Table A1).
oil_density_kg_l <- 0.92
q0_billion_liters <- q0_mt / oil_density_kg_l # ~221 billion L

# Primary: Roberts & Schlenker (2013) staple-food elasticities (Table 1), for supply and demand.
eps_s_rs <- 0.10
eps_d_rs <- -0.05

# Alternative: the same demand elasticity with the land-use model's own one-year supply
# elasticity for vegetable oil (model-supply-curve chunk).
eps_s_model <- eps_model("vegetable_oil")

# For comparison only, not run through the land-use model: Chen et al. (2026). Demand: flexibility
# of -3.523 (Table S1 col 3) inverts to eps_d = -0.284. Supply: long-run 0.10 (palm) and 0.13
# (competing oil crops) (Fig. 2B rows 3-4), weighted by production share as in their eps_S formula.
demand_flexibility_chen <- -3.523
eps_d_chen <- 1 / demand_flexibility_chen
share_palm <- psd_four_oils$production_mt[
  psd_four_oils$Commodity_Description == "Oil, Palm"
] /
  q0_mt
eps_s_chen <- 0.10 * share_palm + 0.13 * (1 - share_palm)

# eps_d is negative, so the multiplier denominator is eps_s + |eps_d|.
m_rs <- 1 / (eps_s_rs - eps_d_rs) # ~6.7
m_model <- 1 / (eps_s_model - eps_d_rs) # ~20
m_chen <- 1 / (eps_s_chen - eps_d_chen) # ~2.5

# Check: the formula should recover each source paper's own headline price effect.
validation <- tibble::tribble(
  ~check                                                        , ~shock_pct , ~m     , ~reported                                  ,
  "Roberts & Schlenker (p. 2277): ethanol mandate = 5% of world calories" , 5.0 , m_rs , "about 30% (p. 2280); 5% x their Table 1 multipliers gives 29-39%",
  "Chen et al. (p. 3): biofuels used 8.5% of vegetable oil, 2002-2018" , 8.5 , m_chen , "21.2% (90% CI: 12.2-28.5%) (p. 3)"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(implied_pct = round(shock_pct * m, 1)) |>
  dplyr::select(check, shock_pct, implied_pct, reported)

knitr::kable(
  validation,
  col.names = c(
    "Check",
    "Demand shift (% of market)",
    "Implied %ΔP (our formula)",
    "Paper's result"
  ),
  caption = paste0(
    "Multipliers: M = ", round(m_rs, 2), " (Roberts & Schlenker) and M = ", round(m_chen, 2),
    " (Chen et al.). With each paper's own elasticities, the formula recovers that paper's headline result."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: derive-price-shock

# %ΔP_t = (D_t / Q0) * M, expressed as a percent. beyond_marginal flags years where the shift
# exceeds 25% of the market, outside the regime where the approximation is reliable.
price_shock <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    vo_demand_billion_liters,
    demand_share_pct = 100 * vo_demand_billion_liters / q0_billion_liters,
    pct_delta_p_rs = demand_share_pct * m_rs,
    pct_delta_p_rs_model = demand_share_pct * m_model,
    beyond_marginal = demand_share_pct > 25
  )

knitr::kable(
  price_shock |>
    dplyr::mutate(beyond_marginal = ifelse(beyond_marginal, "yes", "")),
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "VO demand (billion L)",
    "Share of market (%)",
    "%ΔP, Roberts & Schlenker",
    "%ΔP, emLab model",
    "Beyond marginal"
  ),
  caption = "Vegetable-oil price shock from marine biofuel demand. Both scenarios use Roberts & Schlenker's demand elasticity; 'emLab model' uses the emLab model's own supply elasticity. Years marked 'beyond marginal' are outside the range where the linear approximation holds up."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: price-shock-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

price_shock_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = price_shock$year, scenario = "rs", pct = price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs),
  data.frame(year = price_shock$year, scenario = "model", pct = price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs_model)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(price_shock_long, ggplot2::aes(year, pct, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.8, stroke = 0.8, colour = col_surface) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_scenario, breaks = names(col_scenario), labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_scenario, breaks = names(col_scenario), labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = price_shock$year) +

    x = NULL,

  ) +

```

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-demand
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5

# The vegetable-oil market in 2035: Roberts & Schlenker demand (eps_d = -0.05) before and after
# ICCT's marine demand D, against Roberts & Schlenker's supply (eps_s = 0.10) and the land-use
# model's simulated one-year supply curve. All curves use the price-shock formula's linear
# approximation, %dQ = eps x %dP. The marked equilibria are the price shocks run through the model.
shock_rs <- price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs[price_shock$year == 2035]
shock_model <- price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs_model[price_shock$year == 2035]
d_mt <- price_shock$vo_demand_billion_liters[price_shock$year == 2035] * oil_density_kg_l
veg_1y <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::filter(experiment == "vegetable_oil", years == 1) |>
  dplyr::select(pct_change, extra_mt) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(data.frame(pct_change = 0, extra_mt = 0)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(pct_change)
model_supply_mt <- stats::approxfun(veg_1y$pct_change, veg_1y$extra_mt)

# Where the simulated curve itself crosses 2035 demand: extra supply equals marine demand minus the
# other demand the price rise chokes off.
p_cross_model <- stats::uniroot(
  \(p) model_supply_mt(p) - (d_mt + eps_d_rs * q0_mt * p / 100),
  range(veg_1y$pct_change)
)$root

curve_names <- c(
  "Demand today (ε = −0.05)",
  "Demand with 2035 marine demand",
  "Supply, Roberts & Schlenker (ε = 0.10)",
  paste0("Supply, emLab model (1 year, ε = ", fmt_eps(eps_s_model), ")")
)
p_grid <- seq(-50, 1500, by = 10)
market_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[1], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100)),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[2], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100) + d_mt),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[3], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_s_rs * p_grid / 100)),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[4], p = veg_1y$pct_change, q = q0_mt + veg_1y$extra_mt)
)
market_curves$curve <- factor(market_curves$curve, levels = curve_names)
equilibria <- data.frame(
  q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * c(0, shock_rs, shock_model) / 100) + c(0, d_mt, d_mt),
  p = c(0, shock_rs, shock_model),
  label = c("Today", paste0("+", fmt0(shock_rs), "%"), paste0("+", fmt0(shock_model), "%")),
  hjust = c(-0.3, -0.3, -0.3)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(market_curves, ggplot2::aes(q, p, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, p), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "#0b0b0b", colour = col_surface, stroke = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, p, label = label, hjust = hjust), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3.4, colour = "#0b0b0b"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(c("#8f8d86", "#0b0b0b", col_scenario[["rs"]], col_scenario[["model"]]), curve_names),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = stats::setNames(c("22", "solid", "solid", "solid"), curve_names), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 400, 100)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 410), ylim = c(-50, 1500), expand = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::guides(colour = ggplot2::guide_legend(ncol = 2), linetype = ggplot2::guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "The world vegetable-oil market in 2035",
    x = "Vegetable oil (Mt a year)",
    y = "Change in vegetable-oil price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

The figure shows the 2035 market: Roberts & Schlenker's demand curve before and after ICCT's `r fmt0(d_mt)` Mt of marine demand, and both supply curves. With Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity, prices rise `r fmt0(shock_rs)`%. The model's supply curve is nearly vertical, so other buyers have to give up almost all of the new demand. That takes a rise of `r fmt0(shock_model)`%, a multiplier of `r fmt1(m_model)`, close to the demand-only limit of $1/|\varepsilon_d| = 20$. (The simulated curve itself crosses demand at `r fmt0(p_cross_model)`%, so using the elasticity at baseline prices barely matters.) Neither number is a forecast: the shift is far outside the linear formula's range, and with elasticities this small the answer depends mostly on the shape assumed for the curves. Chen et al.'s elasticities would give `r fmt0(price_shock$demand_share_pct[price_shock$year == 2035] * m_chen)`% ($M \approx$ `r fmt1(m_chen)`). The model's supply paired with the model's own demand elasticity for palm (`r fmt_el(eps_d_model[["Oil, palm"]])`), as its price calculation pairs them, would give `r fmt0(pct_delta_p_model_own)`% ([Appendix C](#sec-model-demand)).

The land-use runs use the 2035 values.

handoff_2035 <- price_shock |>

}

cat(sprintf(

    "2035: VO demand %.0f billion L on a Q0 of %.0f billion L (demand share %.0f%%).\n",
    "Roberts & Schlenker: multiplier %.2f, price shock +%.0f%%.\n",
    "emLab model supply: multiplier %.2f, price shock +%.0f%%."
  ),

### Forest loss {#sec-results-forest}

Extra loss is the difference in forest between the BAU run and a shocked run. It is cumulative, so the last model year gives the total over the whole simulation.

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-global

horizons <- c(2035, 2050, final_year)
global_table <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% horizons) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year),
    carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9,
    area_mha = area_loss / 1e6,
    pct_of_bau_carbon = 100 * carbon_loss / carbon_bau
  )

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = global_table$years_after_shock[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "R&S: Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_gt[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "R&S: Mha" = global_table$area_mha[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "R&S: % of BAU forest carbon" = global_table$pct_of_bau_carbon[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "emLab model: Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_gt[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs_model"],

)

The maps, charts and country table below show the primary scenario.

#### Check: does the cleared land supply the oil? {#sec-results-check}

The price shock and the emLab model only fit together if the land the model clears grows roughly the extra oil the shock assumes. The table compares the two and converts the oil into the supply elasticity the model actually delivers.

```{r}
#| label: land-oil-check

# Extra palm and soybean oil grown on the extra land each scenario clears (01_prepare_data.R's
# per-pixel crop output, totalled by 03_summarise_results.R), against the extra oil supply its
# price shock assumes (eps_s x %dP x Q0). The realized supply elasticity is that extra oil as a
# share of Q0, divided by the price change; realized / assumed = extra oil / assumed extra supply.
check_scenarios <- c(vo_rs = "Roberts & Schlenker", vo_rs_model = "emLab model")
check_shock <- c(vo_rs = shock_rs, vo_rs_model = shock_model)
check_eps <- c(vo_rs = eps_s_rs, vo_rs_model = eps_s_model)
check <- expand.grid(scenario = names(check_scenarios), years = c(1, 15, 25), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
check$cleared_mha <- mapply(\(s, y) gl(s, min(lum$year) + y, "area_loss"), check$scenario, check$years) / 1e6
check$oil_mt <- mapply(
  \(s, y) gl(s, min(lum$year) + y, "extra_palm_oil_t") + soy_oil_per_bean * gl(s, min(lum$year) + y, "extra_soybeans_t"),
  check$scenario, check$years
) / 1e6
check$assumed_mt <- check_eps[check$scenario] * check_shock[check$scenario] / 100 * q0_mt
check$eps_realized <- (check$oil_mt / q0_mt) / (check_shock[check$scenario] / 100)
check <- check[order(match(check$scenario, names(check_scenarios)), check$years), ]
ck <- function(scn, yrs, var) check[[var]][check$scenario == scn & check$years == yrs]

# Least land that would grow the assumed extra supply: all of it palm, at the world's average palm oil yield.
psd_palm <- psd[psd$Commodity_Description == "Oil, Palm" & psd$Market_Year == q0_market_year, ]
palm_oil_yield <- sum(psd_palm$Value[psd_palm$Attribute_Description == "Production"]) /
  sum(psd_palm$Value[psd_palm$Attribute_Description == "Area Harvested"]) # t/ha (both in thousands)
land_needed_mha <- check_eps[["vo_rs"]] * check_shock[["vo_rs"]] / 100 * q0_mt / palm_oil_yield

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Scenario" = check_scenarios[check$scenario],
    "Years after shock" = check$years,
    "Extra forest cleared (Mha)" = fmt1(check$cleared_mha),
    "Oil grown on it (Mt a year)" = formatC(check$oil_mt, format = "f", digits = 2),
    "Extra oil supply the price shock assumes (Mt a year)" = formatC(check$assumed_mt, format = "f", digits = 2),
    "Supply elasticity, realized" = vapply(check$eps_realized, fmt_eps, character(1)),
    "Supply elasticity, assumed" = vapply(check_eps[check$scenario], fmt_eps, character(1)),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = "lrrrrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "Oil grown on the extra land each scenario clears, counted the way the model's own code counts it",
    "(cleared area × cropland share × crop mix × yield; soybeans converted to oil at 11 lb per 60 lb bushel),",
    "against the extra supply the price shock assumes. Realized supply elasticity: that oil as a share of",
    "world production of the four oils, divided by the price change."
  )
)
```

In the primary scenario, the shock assumes the world grows `r fmt1(ck("vo_rs", 1, "assumed_mt"))` Mt a year more vegetable oil and other buyers use `r fmt1(d_mt - ck("vo_rs", 1, "assumed_mt"))` Mt less, together covering the ships' `r fmt0(d_mt)` Mt. Even grown entirely as palm, at the 2024/25 world average of `r formatC(palm_oil_yield, format = "f", digits = 2)` t of oil per hectare [@usdapsd], that new supply needs at least `r fmt0(land_needed_mha)` Mha. The model clears `r fmt1(ck("vo_rs", 15, "cleared_mha"))` Mha more forest than BAU within 15 years and `r fmt1(ck("vo_rs", 25, "cleared_mha"))` Mha within 25, which is the same order. But it counts only `r formatC(ck("vo_rs", 25, "oil_mt"), format = "f", digits = 2)` Mt a year of palm and soybean oil grown on that land after 25 years: `r fmt1(100 * ck("vo_rs", 25, "oil_mt") / ck("vo_rs", 25, "assumed_mt"))`% of the assumed new supply, or `r formatC(ck("vo_rs", 25, "oil_mt") / ck("vo_rs", 25, "cleared_mha"), format = "f", digits = 3)` t per hectare cleared against `r formatC(palm_oil_yield, format = "f", digits = 2)` for palm. As an elasticity, a shock that assumes 0.10 delivers `r fmt_eps(ck("vo_rs", 1, "eps_realized"))` in the first year and `r fmt_eps(ck("vo_rs", 25, "eps_realized"))` after 25 years.

This doesn't undercut the ILUC estimates, which count the carbon in all the extra forest cleared, whatever the land is used for afterwards. A large ILUC value and a tiny supply elasticity are consistent: in the model, a higher price causes a lot of clearing, but little of the cleared land counts as palm or soybean cropland ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)).

The gap has two readings. Either the cleared land grows far more oil than the model counts (`r fmt1(ck("vo_rs", 25, "cleared_mha"))` Mha of palm at average yields would grow `r fmt0(ck("vo_rs", 25, "cleared_mha") * palm_oil_yield)` Mt a year), or most of the new supply comes from land that wasn't forest, higher yields and other oil crops, whose land-use effects our estimate leaves out. The emLab-model scenario is roughly consistent in its first year (`r fmt_eps(ck("vo_rs_model", 1, "eps_realized"))` realized against `r fmt_eps(eps_s_model)` assumed; the curve flattens at high prices), but its supply keeps growing after that.

#### By country and crop

To split the loss by crop, we ran the primary shock on palm alone and on soybeans alone. Palm accounts for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the extra loss and soybeans for `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["soy"]] / sum(crop_split))`%. The two runs add up to the combined run to within `r formatC(abs(interaction_pct), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, so the interaction between them is negligible.

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-country-chart
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5.2

top_n <- 12
top_countries <- rs_final$country[seq_len(top_n)]
other_label <- sprintf("Other %d countries", sum(rs_final$carbon_loss > 0) - top_n)

crop_by_country <- country_final |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = ifelse(country %in% top_countries, country, other_label),
    crop = ifelse(scenario == "vo_rs_palm", "Oil palm", "Soybeans")
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(carbon_loss) / 1e6, .by = c(label, crop)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(label = factor(label, levels = rev(c(top_countries, other_label))))
bar_totals <- crop_by_country |> dplyr::summarise(mt = sum(mt), .by = label)

ggplot2::ggplot(crop_by_country, ggplot2::aes(mt, label)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(
    ggplot2::aes(fill = crop),
    position = ggplot2::position_stack(reverse = TRUE), # palm first, from zero
    width = 0.62, colour = col_surface, linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(data = bar_totals, ggplot2::aes(label = fmt0(mt)), hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2, colour = "#0b0b0b") +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_crop, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +

    title = "Additional forest carbon loss by country and crop",
    subtitle = "Roberts & Schlenker scenario, full horizon",
    x = expression("Mt CO"[2]),
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_report() +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())

country_table <- country_final |>

by_scenario <- function(scn, ...) {
